Where the errors are

Both approaches are most accurate at 12–30 breaths/min, where most windows lie. Below 12 breaths/min the DL model fails (MAE 7.7, 27 windows) and over-estimates, pulled towards the common rates it was trained on. The signal-processing methods degrade as RR approaches half the heart rate, because respiratory signals sampled once per beat cannot represent faster breathing; the DL model degrades less.

Fixing the signal-processing methods

ECG- and PPG-derived respiratory signals carry a 1/f-shaped very-low-frequency background (vasomotion, Mayer waves, posture). On training patients about 20 % of the 4–60 bpm power lies below 8 bpm, against 15–28 % within ±2 bpm of the true rate. The published rules take the largest spectral peak, which is usually that background, so the spectral methods under-estimated by ~13 bpm; the background also inflates the thresholds of CtA and the zero crossings of ZeX.

Corrections, chosen on fold-0 training patients only and identical for PPG and ECG: spectral methods (FTS, WCH, ARS, ARM) pick the peak standing highest above a fitted power-law background (as in aperiodic-component removal for neural spectra, Donoghue et al. 2020); ARP takes the pole with the strongest whitened power instead of the largest modulus; CtA, PKS and ZeX run on a half pre-whitened signal; CtO is unchanged. The band keeps its 4 bpm floor. Below, both rules on the held-out patients (smart fusion; coverage = windows where BW, AM and FM agree).

Sample windows

Four held-out windows, chosen automatically: a typical one, the fastest breathing relative to heart rate, the slowest breathing and the largest DL error. Each figure shows, on one time axis, what the methods look at: R peaks (▲) and PPG pulse peaks/onsets (▲▼) from which the respiratory signals are built, the impedance breaths (●) that define the reference, the derived BW/AM/FM signals with the breaths CtO accepts, and the PPG spectra with the 1/f background (dashed), the published pick (orange, dotted), the corrected pick (blue) and the reference (grey). Interactive versions with ECG spectra are in notebook 03.

Fast breathing near HR/2

About two beats per breath: the derived signals are sampled near their Nyquist limit. Spectral methods still find the peak just below HR/2; breath counters miss breaths because each cycle is only a couple of samples long. Reference 42.1 bpm, DL 40.5 bpm, HR 83 (RR/HR 0.50). PPG spectral methods, median: 41.6 bpm as published; 41.6 bpm corrected.

Trends over whole recordings

Every 60-s window of the PPG test patients' recordings (30-s steps), including windows whose reference failed its quality checks. Clinically, following a patient's changes matters as much as each value. Trending ability is scored with four-quadrant analysis (Critchley et al. 2010): for windows 5 minutes apart, does the estimate move in the same direction as the reference? Pairs with a reference change under 2 bpm are excluded; 90 % concordance is the usual bar.

Data and reference

456,754 sixty-second windows from 242 patients (3,811 h of monitor recording). The impedance reference passes quality checks in 64% of windows; 47% are usable with PPG and 63% with ECG. Reference RR has median 24.5 breaths/min (5–95 %: 17–36); RR/HR has median 0.28, and 5% of windows exceed 0.4.

What was wrong in the 2023 pipeline

Every stage had at least one defect that invalidates its results; the code and its outputs are kept in archive/ with a per-file list in archive/README.md. Results produced before October 2026 should not be cited.

StageDefectEffect
LabelsPhilips MPDataExport.csv rows carry one field more than the header, so NOM_RESP_RATE read by name is the heart rate (median 137).Targets were heart rates
LabelsLabel computed over 60 s of reference, input = last 3,000 samples assuming 100 Hz.Input and label covered different time spans
SplitPatients 001 and 004 used the identical recording for train and validation; other “validation” files were other days of the same patients; windows drawn with replacement.Validation scores were leaked
DL input0.5–3.5 Hz band-pass plus 2nd derivative before the spectrogram.99.9 % of respiratory-band power removed
DL input2.56-s STFT window, 1.28-s hop, 0–50 Hz axis resized to 224 px; dB ÷ max then ToPILImage.Rates > 23 bpm aliased; respiration in 2 % of rows; pixel values wrapped mod 256

What replaced it

  1. Read the GE monitor export (ECG, Pleth, thoracic impedance on one clock, 300 Hz); split at gaps; resample to ECG 250 Hz, PPG 100 Hz, impedance 25 Hz (data_prep/).
  2. Window into 60-s windows with a 30-s stride. Reference = breath-by-breath rate (count-adv) on the impedance over exactly the window; kept only when time- and frequency-domain estimates agree within 3 bpm and the channel is not clipped, flat or bursting.
  3. Quality-check the PPG/ECG window: no clipping or flat-line, plausible HR, ≤ 20 % rejected beats.
  4. Extract baseline wander, amplitude and frequency modulation from detected beats (Charlton 2016; Karlen 2013), resample to 4 Hz, band-pass 4–60 breaths/min (estimate_rr/).
  5. Signal processing: nine estimators (CtO, CtA, PKS, ZeX, FTS, WCH, ARS, ARM, ARP) per respiratory signal, fused by smart fusion or median, with a correction for the very-low-frequency background (see the fix); the published rules remain available.
  6. Deep learning: log-power spectrograms of the three respiratory signals (16-s STFT, 1-s hop, 0.94-bpm bins) → small CNN (0.4 M parameters) → distribution over 4–60 breaths/min, trained with Gaussian soft labels; estimate = its mean (dl/).
  7. Evaluate on patients never used for training or model selection: MAE, per-patient MAE, Bland–Altman, coverage, errors by RR range and RR/HR ratio (common/, scripts/).

Unit tests on synthetic ECG, PPG and impedance signals cover every estimator, beat detection, reference quality rules, splits and the DL features (python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .).

Caveats and open questions

  • One fold. These numbers come from fold 0 of 5; the spread across folds is not known yet.
  • Monitor PPG, not the wearable. The input is the bedside monitor's Pleth. The wearable SmartCare PPG and Faros ECG in the same folders are not aligned yet; their header clocks differ by 7 h and must be checked first.
  • Selected windows. Only windows with a clean, regular impedance trace are scored (64%). Irregular breathing, apnoea and motion are under-represented, so accuracy on all windows will be lower.
  • Possible ventilated patients. One test patient's reference sits at 27.9–28.1 breaths/min for half of 25 hours, as a ventilator set rate would. Ventilation status should be taken from the records and those patients analysed separately.
  • Slow breathing. Fewer than 1 % of windows are below 12 breaths/min. The DL model fails there, and so does the low-frequency correction: when breathing itself is below about 8 breaths/min it sits inside the background the fix discounts, and the published spectral rules do better (see the slowest-breathing sample window).
  • Ambiguous labels. Irregular breathing can pass the reference rules: the largest-DL-error sample window has breath intervals of 2–8.5 s and a CV of 0.33, under the 0.5 limit. Tightening the limit to 0.3 would drop 6.6 % of accepted windows.
  • Correction chosen on one fold. The very-low-frequency corrections were chosen on fold-0 training patients; folds 1–4 will show whether they hold.

Next steps

  1. Finish ECG and raw-STFT runs, then folds 1–4 for mean ± SD across folds.
  2. Mark ventilated periods from clinical records; report them separately.
  3. Align the wearable PPG/ECG to the monitor clock (HR cross-correlation) and test the monitor-trained model on wearable signals.
  4. Add low-rate training examples (re-weighting or augmentation) and evaluate 30-s windows.
  5. Re-download the 24EIb Philips data and add a reader for it.
